title: Abuse, DDoS, bots and privacy
scopeHtml:
Scope: WAF, rate limits, DDoS defence, bot handling, GDPR basics, PII handling.

Scope: WAF, rate limits, DDoS defence, bot handling, GDPR basics, PII handling.

notes.title: The abuse landscape
notes.html:
Any public endpoint will be abused: by scrapers, credential-stuffers, spammers, fraudsters and floods. Abuse is not a bug in your code, it is the normal behaviour of an open internet, so protection belongs in the design.

Main types and what they target:

  • Volumetric DDoS (L3/L4): saturate bandwidth (SYN floods, UDP amplification). Needs a big network to absorb.
  • Application-layer DDoS (L7): many valid-looking HTTP requests to expensive endpoints (search, login).
  • Credential stuffing: reuse leaked username/password pairs from other sites against your login.
  • Scraping and inventory hoarding: bots copy content or buy all tickets.
  • Spam / fake accounts / promo abuse: free-trial farming, referral fraud.
  • Enumeration: walking ids or probing "does this email exist?".

Worked example. Normal traffic is 2k requests/s. An L7 attacker sends 200k requests/s to /search, which costs 20 ms of DB time each. That needs 4,000 DB-cores of work; you would fall over in seconds. The CDN cache, a rate limit, and a bot challenge on /search cut it to near zero.

Industry examples. GitHub survived a 1.35 Tbps memcached-amplification DDoS in 2018 using Akamai Prophylexic; Cloudflare reported attacks above 70 million requests/s in 2023 (HTTP/2 rapid reset, confirm exact figures); Ticketmaster fights scalper bots daily; Twitter and Reddit rate-limit scrapers.

Decision gravity. Buying DDoS protection (CDN/cloud shield) is reversible and cheap compared with building capacity. Designing public endpoints to be cheap or cacheable is a one-way architectural advantage.

Everyday analogy. A shop front: fences and bouncers outside, a ticket counter inside, and a cashier who can refuse a customer who orders absurdly.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "add more servers"; attackers outspend you.
  • Treating only DDoS as abuse and ignoring slow "legit-looking" abuse such as scraping.

notes.title: Rate limiting algorithms
notes.html:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a key (IP, user, API key, tenant) can make in a window. It protects fairness, cost and stability.

Algorithms:

  • Fixed window: count per minute. Simple, but allows a burst of 2x at the boundary (100 at 12:00:59, 100 at 12:01:00).
  • Sliding window log: store timestamps; exact, but memory heavy.
  • Sliding window counter: weighted blend of current and previous window; good, cheap approximation.
  • Token bucket: bucket of capacity B refilled at R tokens/s; each request takes one. Allows bursts up to B, average R. The most common choice (AWS API Gateway, Stripe).
  • Leaky bucket: requests drain at a constant rate; smooths output (queue-like).
  • Concurrency limit: cap in-flight requests (good for expensive work).
-- Redis Lua: atomic token bucket (KEYS[1]=key, ARGV: rate, capacity, now, cost)
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 't', 'ts')
local t = tonumber(d[1]) or ARGV[2]
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or ARGV[3]
t = math.min(ARGV[2], t + (ARGV[3]-ts) * ARGV[1])
if t < tonumber(ARGV[4]) then return 0 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 't', t-ARGV[4], 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120)
return 1

Worked example. 5M users, limit 100 requests/min each. State per key: 16 B key + 16 B value = about 50 B with overhead, so 5M x 50 B = 250 MB, one Redis node. Rate-limit checks at 100k/s need 100k Redis ops/s, and so a cluster or local in-memory counters synced periodically at larger scale.

Industry examples. Stripe uses token buckets with several limiter types (request rate, concurrency, load shedding for non-critical traffic); GitHub API 5,000 requests/hour/user with X-RateLimit-* headers; Envoy has a global rate limit service; Nginx limit_req is leaky bucket.

Decision gravity. Algorithm and key choice are reversible. The big call is where: edge (cheap, coarse, protects everything) vs per-service (fine-grained, needs shared state). Also fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down: most choose fail-open for general APIs and fail-closed for login.

Everyday analogy. A bucket that fills with tickets at a steady drip; you can spend a handful at once, but not forever.

Common interview traps.

  • Race conditions with GET then SET (use Lua or INCR atomically).
  • Limiting only by IP (NAT'd offices and mobile carriers share IPs; botnets rotate them). Combine IP, account, device and API key.
  • Returning 500 instead of 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After.

notes.title: Distributed rate limiting and load shedding
notes.html:
With many gateway nodes, a limit must be enforced globally or approximately. Three patterns:

  1. Central store (Redis): exact, adds about 1 ms and a dependency.
  2. Local limits divided by N: each of N nodes gets limit/N. No network, but unfair when load is skewed.
  3. Gossip / periodic sync (approximate): each node counts locally and reports every 100 ms. Fast and mostly correct.

Load shedding is the last line: when the server is overloaded (CPU above 85%, queue deep), reject low-priority requests early with 503 instead of timing out everything. Prioritise: health checks and payments over analytics and search.

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;   # 10m holds about 160k IPs
server { location /api/ { limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay; limit_req_status 429; } }

Worked example. 20 gateways, limit 1,000 req/min/user. Local-divided: 50 each. A user whose traffic hits only 2 gateways is capped at 100/min, not 1,000, a clear unfairness. Use sticky hashing by user to one gateway, or the Redis approach.

Industry examples. Netflix concurrency-limits library and Zuul adaptive shedding; Google SRE "criticality" labels for shedding; Stripe load shedder reserves capacity for critical requests; Cloudflare rate limiting at the edge.

Decision gravity. Shedding policy is reversible config; building it from day one avoids cascading failure (retry storms turn a blip into an outage).

Everyday analogy. A nightclub at capacity: VIPs and staff go in, the rest wait outside rather than packing the room until nobody can dance.

Common interview traps.

  • Clients retrying instantly on 429 and amplifying load. Specify exponential backoff with jitter.
  • No separate quotas for abusive tenants vs normal ones.

notes.title: DDoS defence
notes.html:
Absorb at the edge, filter bad traffic early, and make the origin hard to reach and cheap to serve.

Layers:

  • Anycast CDN / scrubbing network (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield/CloudFront, Google Cloud Armor): one IP announced from 200+ locations, so an attack spreads across the globe and each site absorbs a slice. Capacity: multi-Tbps.
  • L3/L4: SYN cookies, ingress filtering, drop UDP you do not use, never expose amplifiable services (open DNS resolvers, memcached on UDP).
  • L7: cache aggressively, rate limit per IP and per fingerprint, challenge suspicious clients, protect expensive endpoints, set short timeouts (Slowloris defence).
  • Origin protection: firewall the origin to accept only CDN IP ranges (or private link), so attackers cannot bypass the shield.
  • Autoscale carefully with a budget cap; otherwise attackers inflate your cloud bill (economic DoS).

Worked example. A 500 Gbps UDP flood against a 10 Gbps origin link is dead on arrival; against an anycast network with 200 Tbps total capacity across 300 sites it is about 1.7 Gbps per site (assuming even spread), invisible. Page that is cacheable for 10 s turns 200k requests/s into 1 origin request per edge per 10 s.

Industry examples. GitHub 2018 (1.35 Tbps, mitigated by pushing traffic to scrubbers within 10 min); Dyn 2016 (Mirai botnet of IoT cameras took down Twitter, Netflix and Spotify DNS); Google Cloud Armor blocked a 398M requests/s attack in 2023 (rapid reset).

Decision gravity. Hiding the origin IP is an early, one-time choice; if the origin IP ever leaks you may need to renumber. Multi-provider DNS (so one DNS provider is not a single point of failure, the Dyn lesson) is cheap insurance.

Everyday analogy. A stadium with many gates, outer security lines, and VIP entrances only staff know; a mob cannot all push through one door.

Common interview traps.

  • Scaling the origin instead of putting a shield in front.
  • Leaving the origin reachable directly by IP.
  • Forgetting DNS as a target and as a single point of failure.

notes.title: WAF: web application firewall
notes.html:
A WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks known-bad patterns (SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, bad bots) before they hit your app. It works at L7, usually as part of the CDN or load balancer.

Mechanism: rule sets (OWASP Core Rule Set, AWS Managed Rules, Cloudflare Managed), each rule scores or blocks requests that match signatures (' OR 1=1--, ../../etc/passwd, known scanner user agents). Modes: detect/log only first, then block. Add custom rules: geo blocks, IP reputation, rate-based rules, "block POST /login without a valid header". Virtual patching: block an exploit for a fresh CVE in hours while the real fix goes through your release cycle.

{
  "Name": "login-rate",
  "Statement": {"RateBasedStatement": {"Limit": 100, "AggregateKeyType": "IP"}},
  "Action": {"Block": {}},
  "VisibilityConfig": {"SampledRequestsEnabled": true}
}

Worked example. Rolling out: week 1 run OWASP CRS in log-only, 0.4% of legitimate requests flag (false positives, for example a rich-text editor posting <script> samples); tune exclusions; week 2 enable blocking for the high-confidence rules; keep sampling to find drift. Adds about 1 to 5 ms of latency.

Industry examples. AWS WAF (used with CloudFront/ALB), Cloudflare WAF, ModSecurity with OWASP CRS on Nginx, Akamai Kona. Capital One 2019 showed WAFs do not fix over-privileged internal roles.

Decision gravity. A WAF is reversible and quick to deploy. Danger: a false-positive rule blocking real customers silently. It is a safety net, not a substitute for input validation and patching.

Everyday analogy. An airport scanner that looks at every bag for known dangerous items; it will miss novel threats and occasionally flags a harmless bag.

Common interview traps.

  • "We have a WAF so injection is solved."
  • Going straight to block mode without a log-only period.
  • Not inspecting what the WAF cannot see (E2EE or encrypted payloads, gRPC/binary bodies).

notes.title: Bot detection and mitigation
notes.html:
Bots are automated clients; some are good (Googlebot), many are not. The goal is to make abuse expensive, not to block all automation.

Signals, cheap to costly:

  1. Reputation: IP ranges of data centers and VPN/proxy services, known bad ASNs, threat feeds.
  2. Behaviour: request rate, no cookies, perfectly regular timing, sequential id walking, no mouse/touch events.
  3. Fingerprinting: TLS fingerprint (JA3/JA4), HTTP/2 settings, header order, browser/device attributes.
  4. Challenges: JavaScript proof-of-work, CAPTCHA (reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Cloudflare Turnstile), mobile attestation (Play Integrity, Apple App Attest).
  5. Business logic: per-account limits, purchase limits, queueing (virtual waiting room), step-up MFA, honeypot fields, one-time tokens.

Combine into a risk score and respond in tiers: allow, throttle, challenge, block, or tarpit.

Worked example. Sneaker drop: 1M real users, 5M bot requests for 10k pairs. Virtual waiting room admits 2k users/min in random order, per-account purchase limit 1, one card per order, challenge only on suspicious scores. Real users see a queue; bots lose their speed advantage.

Industry examples. Cloudflare Bot Management, Akamai, DataDome, PerimeterX; Ticketmaster Verified Fan; Google Play Integrity for Android apps; Instagram and LinkedIn aggressively detect scrapers. Well-behaved crawlers are verified by reverse DNS and robots.txt obeyed.

Decision gravity. It is an arms race; build it as a replaceable layer with tunable rules. Over-aggressive blocking hurts conversion and accessibility (CAPTCHAs are a barrier).

Everyday analogy. A shop that notices someone filling a trolley with 200 identical items and asks for ID and a limit, while greeting normal shoppers as usual.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying only on IP blocks.
  • CAPTCHA everywhere (poor UX, and solvable by farms for about $1 per 1,000).
  • Ignoring mobile apps: attestation, not CAPTCHA, is the right tool there.

notes.title: Account abuse: credential stuffing and fraud
notes.html:
Credential stuffing tries billions of leaked pairs; even a 0.1% hit rate yields many accounts. Defences must work at login and after.

Controls:

  • Per-IP and per-account limits, with exponential backoff; do not hard-lock accounts (attackers could lock out victims); soft-lock with step-up verification.
  • Breached-password checks (k-anonymity API of Have I Been Pwned), MFA / passkeys, new-device and impossible-travel checks.
  • Uniform responses: same message and timing for "unknown user" vs "wrong password" to prevent enumeration.
  • Risk-based auth: low risk flows straight through; high risk (new country, Tor) adds OTP.
  • Fraud signals: device id, velocity (cards per account per hour), email domain reputation, disposable email lists.

Worked example. Attacker has 10M leaked pairs, rotating 100k IPs; each IP does 100 tries/day. Per-IP limits barely help. A per-account limit of 5 failures/hour plus an IP reputation score plus a device cookie cuts successful takeovers from about 0.5% of tries (50k accounts) to under 1,000.

Industry examples. Netflix, Disney+ and Spotify credential-stuffing waves; Okta "Credential Stuffing" detections; Stripe Radar (ML scoring each charge); Uber and Swiggy promo-code fraud rules; Paytm and PhonePe velocity checks.

Decision gravity. Fraud systems are reversible and iterative; the hard-to-reverse decision is logging enough signals (device, IP, timing) from the start to feed ML later.

Everyday analogy. A bank teller who remembers you; unusual behaviour (a new city and a huge withdrawal) triggers extra questions.

Common interview traps.

  • Account lockout as the only control (denial of service on victims).
  • Different error messages that reveal whether the account exists.

notes.title: GDPR basics
notes.html:
GDPR is the EU law giving people control over their personal data; it applies to anyone handling EU residents' data, wherever the company is. Fines up to 4% of global annual turnover or 20M euros, whichever is higher.

Core ideas for engineers:

  • Lawful basis for processing (consent, contract, legitimate interest, legal obligation).
  • Data subject rights: access (give a copy), rectification, erasure ("right to be forgotten"), portability (machine-readable export), objection, restriction.
  • Data minimisation and purpose limitation: collect only what you need, use it only for the stated reason.
  • Storage limitation: retention periods; delete when no longer needed.
  • Security (Article 32) and breach notification within 72 hours to the regulator.
  • Privacy by design/default, DPIA for risky processing, DPO where required.
  • Cross-border transfers: need safeguards (SCCs, adequacy decisions); data residency is often required in design (EU data stays in EU regions).
  • Similar laws: CCPA/CPRA (California), DPDP Act 2023 (India), LGPD (Brazil). Confirm legal details with counsel.

Worked example. Erasure request for user 42: 12 systems hold data (OLTP DB, search index, caches, warehouse, S3 logs, backups, analytics vendor, support tool). SLA: complete within 30 days. Design: one user_id key everywhere, a deletion event consumed by each system, a ledger proving completion. Backups: either wait for natural expiry (documented, for example 35 days) or crypto-shred.

Industry examples. Meta fined 1.2B euros (2023) for transfers to the US; Amazon 746M euros (2021); Google and Apple provide data export tools ("Takeout", privacy portal); Spotify and Airbnb run deletion pipelines driven by events.

Decision gravity. Retrofitting erasure into a system with copied data everywhere is a very expensive one-way mess. Designing data lineage and a single subject identifier early is cheap.

Everyday analogy. A library that must show you every card it has on you, correct it, and destroy it on request, including the copies in the back room.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting backups, logs, caches and analytics copies in an erasure design.
  • Hard-deleting rows that other legal rules (tax records) require you to keep: erasure has exceptions.
  • Treating GDPR as legal-only; it dictates architecture (residency, retention, consent storage).

notes.title: PII handling and data classification
notes.html:
PII (personally identifiable information) is anything that identifies a person: name, email, phone, address, IP, device id, government id, biometrics, location. Handle it with the fewest copies, the shortest life and the tightest access.

Practices:

  • Classify data: public, internal, confidential, restricted (PII, payment, health). Tag columns and fields.
  • Minimise and isolate: keep PII in one service/DB (a "PII vault"); other systems store an opaque user_id or token.
  • Tokenisation vs pseudonymisation vs anonymisation: tokens map back via the vault; pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR; truly anonymised data (not re-identifiable) is out of scope but hard to achieve.
  • Mask in non-prod and logs: a***@gmail.com, last 4 digits; never copy prod PII into staging.
  • Access control + audit: just-in-time access, every read logged; column-level encryption for the most sensitive fields.
  • Retention jobs: TTL deletes (Cassandra TTL, S3 lifecycle, partition drops).
  • Crypto-shredding: encrypt each user's data with a per-user key; delete the key to make all copies, backups included, unreadable.
  • PCI-DSS for card data (use Stripe/Adyen tokens so card numbers never touch your servers), HIPAA for US health data.
-- retention by partition drop (cheap, vs row-by-row delete)
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2025_01;
DROP TABLE events_2025_01;
-- masked view for analysts
CREATE VIEW users_masked AS SELECT id, left(email,1)||'***@'||split_part(email,'@',2) AS email FROM users;

Worked example. 100M users, per-user encryption key (32 B) = 3.2 GB of keys in KMS/DB; deleting 10k users' keys per day makes their data in S3 logs and backups instantly unreadable, with no scanning of petabytes.

Industry examples. Stripe tokenises cards; Apple differential privacy; Uber and Airbnb run internal data catalogs that tag PII columns for automated deletion; log pipelines scrub emails and phone numbers via regex before indexing.

Decision gravity. The PII vault and tokenisation decision is cheap early, nearly impossible to undo after PII has spread to 40 services. Crypto-shredding must be designed in at write time.

Everyday analogy. Keeping passports in the hotel safe and giving staff a room number, not the passport copy.

Common interview traps.

  • Logging PII or tokens (log pipelines are rarely access-controlled like databases).
  • Using production data in test environments.
  • Believing hashing an email makes it anonymous (hashes of emails are easily reversed by guessing).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Expect abuse: volumetric DDoS, L7 floods, credential stuffing, scraping, fake accounts. Layer defences from CDN to app.
  • Rate limit with token bucket (burst plus average), atomic in Redis, keyed by IP + account + API key; return 429 with Retry-After; clients back off with jitter; decide fail-open or closed.
  • Shed low-priority load before collapse; keep critical paths reserved.
  • DDoS: anycast CDN/scrubbing, cache, lock the origin to the shield, redundant DNS, budget caps on autoscale.
  • WAF: managed rules, log-only first, virtual patching; a safety net not a fix.
  • Bots: score signals (reputation, behaviour, fingerprint), challenge in tiers, attest mobile apps, use waiting rooms and per-account limits.
  • Credential stuffing: per-account limits, breached-password checks, MFA/passkeys, uniform error messages.
  • GDPR: lawful basis, user rights (access, erasure, portability), minimisation, retention, 72-hour breach notice, residency. Design deletion across all copies.
  • PII: classify, isolate in a vault, tokenise, mask, audit, retention TTLs, crypto-shredding; never log it.

questions.promptHtml: Compare fixed window, sliding window, token bucket and leaky bucket rate limiting. Which would you pick for a public API?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Rate limiting is in almost every design; the signal is knowing burst behaviour and memory cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fixed window is simplest but allows 2x bursts at window edges. Sliding window log is exact but stores every timestamp. Sliding window counter approximates cheaply. Token bucket allows controlled bursts at a steady average and is my default for APIs. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate, good for protecting a downstream.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fixed window (100/min): 100 requests at 12:00:59 + 100 at 12:01:00 = 200 in 2 s
Token bucket: capacity 100, refill 100/min -> burst up to 100, then ~1.67/s
Leaky bucket: queue drains at a fixed rate; excess dropped or delayed
Sliding counter: count = cur + prev * (1 - elapsed/window)   (approx, 2 counters per key)
  • Memory per key: fixed 1 counter; token bucket 2 numbers (tokens, last refill); sliding log N timestamps (100 requests = about 800 B per user, 10M users = 8 GB).
  • Key choice matters as much as the algorithm: per user, per API key, per IP, per endpoint; return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers.
  • Token bucket lazy refill: on each request compute tokens = min(cap, tokens + (now-last)*rate).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def allow(bucket, now, rate, cap):
    bucket.tokens = min(cap, bucket.tokens + (now - bucket.last) * rate)
    bucket.last = now
    if bucket.tokens >= 1:
        bucket.tokens -= 1
        return True
    return False

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixed window for anything where a 2x boundary burst hurts.
  • Limiting by IP only (NAT, mobile carriers share IPs; attackers rotate them).
  • Silent drops without Retry-After; clients then hammer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Different limits for tiers? -> Per-plan config keyed by API key; bucket capacity and refill differ.
  2. Burst vs sustained? -> Token bucket capacity = burst, refill = sustained.
  3. Where does it run? -> Gateway or sidecar with a shared store (Redis) for global limits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: names the algorithms. Senior: quantifies the burst and memory, chooses keys, and designs headers and client behaviour.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fixed-window limiter let a partner send double the quota across the minute boundary every minute and overloaded a fragile downstream.

questions.promptHtml: What are the GDPR basics an engineer must design for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Privacy requirements shape data models, retention and deletion; ignoring them is expensive to retrofit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Lawful basis and consent for processing, data minimisation, purpose limitation, user rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability), breach notification within 72 hours, and privacy by design. For engineers that means knowing where personal data lives, being able to export and delete it per user, setting retention limits and keeping an audit trail.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Personal data = anything identifying a person directly or indirectly (email, IP, device id, location).
  • Rights have deadlines (about one month, verify with counsel). You need a user-to-data map across DBs, caches, search indexes, analytics, logs, backups and third parties.
  • Erasure vs backups: delete from live systems and let backups age out within a stated period, while ensuring restores re-apply deletions.
  • Controls: data minimisation (do not collect it), encryption, access control, pseudonymisation, regional storage when required, processor agreements with vendors.
  • Breach: detect, assess, notify the authority within 72 hours where required.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Deleting from the main DB but forgetting search index, analytics, data warehouse and logs.
  • Keeping data "just in case" forever.
  • Treating pseudonymised data as non-personal.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you implement the right to erasure? -> User-id keyed deletion job fanning out to every store, tracked to completion.
  2. What is data residency? -> Keeping data in specific regions, may influence region design.
  3. Is consent always required? -> No, other lawful bases exist (contract, legal obligation); legal decides.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists rights. Senior: a data inventory, deletion fan-out, retention automation and backup handling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams discover during a deletion request that the user's email lives in 14 systems nobody had documented.

questions.contextHtml:
A Redis-backed fixed-window limiter (100 requests per minute per API key) is deployed on 12 gateway pods. Ops notes some keys get no limit at all and Redis memory slowly grows with keys with no TTL.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean allow(String key) {
    long count = redis.incr("rl:" + key);          // step 1
    if (count == 1) {
        redis.expire("rl:" + key, 60);             // step 2
    }
    return count <= 100;
}
fun allow(key: String): Boolean {
    val count = redis.incr("rl:$key")              // step 1
    if (count == 1L) redis.expire("rl:$key", 60)   // step 2
    return count <= 100
}
questions.promptHtml: What bugs exist and how do you fix them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, INCR is atomic." Misses that two commands are not atomic together.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Redis connection pooled and can calls fail between steps? Is this fail-open or fail-closed on Redis errors?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run a one-off scan for rl:* keys with TTL -1 and set expiry; those keys block users forever once above 100.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) crash/timeout between INCR and EXPIRE leaves a key without TTL; counter never resets so the user is blocked permanently (or limit effectively infinite if the key is cleaned manually); (2) fixed window boundary burst; (3) Redis error handling returns exceptions and blocks traffic.
  4. How I'd verify: redis-cli --scan --pattern 'rl:*' plus TTL, fault injection killing the pod between calls.
  5. Root cause: A two-step non-atomic operation.
  6. Fix: Make it one atomic unit with a Lua script or SET key 0 EX 60 NX first, or token bucket in a Lua script.
-- Lua (runs atomically)
local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if c == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
return c

Decide fail-open or fail-closed explicitly (usually fail-open for general APIs, fail-closed for login). 7. Prevention: Chaos test for partial failure; metric for keys without TTL; code review rule: multi-command invariants go into scripts. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lua blocks Redis briefly, so keep scripts tiny. I would not use MULTI/EXEC alone since it does not branch on the INCR result.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Clock skew between pods? -> The window is TTL-based on Redis time, so pods' clocks do not matter.
  • 10x traffic? -> Shard by key, use local pre-limiters, see distributed limiting.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A TTL-less counter permanently blocked a paying customer for two weeks until someone noticed a growing key count.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Misses it.
  • Hire: Finds the atomicity gap, uses Lua.
  • Strong hire: Adds fail-open/closed policy, orphan-key detection and chaos test.

questions.contextHtml:
Tuesday 11:20. Normal traffic is 3k rps. Suddenly 140k rps hits /search?q=<random>. Origin CPU 100%, DB connection pool exhausted. Edge logs:

requests/s by country: 62% from 40 countries, each under 3% share
user agents: 9 distinct, all "Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/118"
query strings: all unique (cache hit ratio 0.1%)
bandwidth: 280 Mbps (small)  -> not a volumetric flood
TLS fingerprint (JA3): 3 values cover 90% of requests
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate and design for the next one.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more servers", which pays the attacker's bill, or blocks by country and cuts off real users.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have a CDN/WAF? Which endpoints are expensive? Do we need anonymous search?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable the CDN's under-attack mode or rate limits on /search, challenge suspicious fingerprints (JA3 clusters), require a cheap proof such as a token for anonymous search, serve stale or reduced results, protect the DB with a concurrency limit and load shedding.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) L7 application flood with cache-busting queries; (2) botnet using real browsers (UA identical, 3 JA3 values); (3) volumetric (no; bandwidth is small).
  4. How I'd verify: Edge analytics grouped by JA3, ASN, path; DB slow query log; check the origin is directly reachable (bypassing CDN).
  5. Root cause: An expensive uncached endpoint exposed anonymously with no per-client limit, and origin reachable.
  6. Fix: Short term: rate limit per IP and per fingerprint, block JA3 clusters, challenge, normalise/ignore random query params for cache, bounded DB pool plus queue with timeouts. Long term: lock origin to CDN IP ranges, autoscaling with caps, per-request cost limits, degrade features gracefully.
  7. Prevention: Baseline alarms (rps, cache hit ratio drop), runbook, DDoS protection contract, load tests including cache-busting patterns.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Challenges add friction for real users; use them adaptively. I would not scale the origin to absorb the flood (cost and DB bottleneck) and would not geo-block 40 countries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Attackers solve the challenge? -> Combine signals: behaviour, fingerprints, reputation, per-account limits.
  • What about a volumetric flood? -> Absorb at an anycast CDN/scrubbing provider; origin cannot.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Autoscaling tripled the bill during an attack while the DB, the real bottleneck, still fell over.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scale up or country block.
  • Hire: Rate limit, challenge, protect DB.
  • Strong hire: Classifies L7 vs volumetric from metrics, origin lockdown, cost awareness, graceful degradation.

questions.contextHtml: Your org is putting a managed WAF (OWASP core rule set) in front of an API at 8k rps and a checkout flow. Last time a team enabled blocking mode in one go and lost 3% of legitimate orders for two hours because a rule flagged JSON bodies containing SELECT-like product names and a SOAP integration. Security wants coverage in two weeks.
questions.promptHtml: How do you roll out the WAF safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Enable all rules in block mode and fix what breaks."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints are most sensitive? What are known odd payloads (rich text, SOAP, file uploads)? Who owns exceptions? What is the rollback time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; begin in detection (count/log) mode so no traffic is blocked.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (where false positives come from): (1) free-text fields; (2) encoded payloads and uploads; (3) legacy partner integrations; (4) API clients with odd headers.
  4. How I'd verify: Run in count mode for 1 to 2 weeks, aggregate matched rules by path and rule id, sample payloads, estimate false-positive rate against known good traffic (for example synthetic and replayed requests).
  5. Root cause of past failure: No staged rollout and no per-endpoint tuning.
  6. Fix (plan): Count mode, tune: exclusions scoped to path and field, not global rule disable; move rules to block one category at a time (SQLi, XSS, protocol), starting with high-confidence ones; canary 5% of traffic; automatic rollback when 4xx rate on checkout rises; keep rate limits and bot rules separate.
  7. Prevention: WAF config in version control with review, replay-based regression tests before rule updates, dashboards for blocked-by-rule, an exception expiry date.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: WAF is a safety net; it will not fix broken authz or business-logic bugs. I would not disable a whole rule group for one false positive, and not skip the app-level fixes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• New rule set version? -> Test in count mode first.
  • Latency cost? -> Typically a few ms; verify with the vendor.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A global "disable SQLi rules" exclusion added during a panic stayed for a year until a pen test noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang block.
  • Hire: Count mode then tuned block.
  • Strong hire: Scoped exclusions, canary and rollback, replay tests and knows WAF limits.

questions.contextHtml:
A retail site sees 35% of product-page traffic from non-human clients. Marketing says "stop the scrapers", but SEO needs Googlebot, partners use an affiliate feed, and a price comparison site is a customer. Logs:

IP 198.51.100.7 : 4,800 req/hour, sequential product ids, no cookies, UA "python-requests/2.31"
residential proxy pool: 20,000 IPs, each 8 req/hour, headless Chrome, same navigation pattern
real users: median 14 pages/session
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: IP blocklist only; residential proxies make that useless, and Googlebot may get blocked.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What harm: server cost, price scraping, inventory hoarding? Which bots are allowed? Is a login or API acceptable for partners? What false-positive tolerance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the obvious (python-requests, high-volume IP) and allow verified Googlebot via reverse-DNS check.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) naive scrapers (easy signals); (2) distributed headless browsers behind residential proxies (low per-IP rate); (3) partners misusing page scraping instead of the feed.
  4. How I'd verify: Session analysis: navigation order, timing, missing assets (no CSS/JS fetch), device fingerprint clusters, honeypot links.
  5. Root cause: Valuable data publicly available with no friction and no business-approved channel.
  6. Fix: Layered: allowlist verified good bots; official feed/API with keys for partners (rate limited, ToS); behavioural scoring plus device fingerprint and challenges for risky sessions; rate limit by session and fingerprint, not just IP; serve decoys or slower responses to suspected bots; for price protection consider requiring login for bulk access.
  7. Prevention: Metrics: bot share, challenge pass rate, conversion by segment; review monthly as attackers adapt.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Aggressive challenges hurt conversion and accessibility; tune against measured conversion. I would not promise to stop scraping entirely; the goal is raising cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Captcha solving farms? -> Cheap, so captcha is a speed bump; rely on behaviour and economics.
  • Legal? -> ToS and legal action are part of the toolkit; consult counsel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Blocking one IP range took out a mobile carrier's NAT and thousands of legitimate customers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: IP blocklist.
  • Hire: Clarifies business goal; layers signals.
  • Strong hire: Partner channel, good-bot verification, conversion-aware tuning and economics.

questions.promptHtml: How do you do rate limiting across many gateway nodes, and how is load shedding different from rate limiting?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A single-node limiter is easy; senior answers handle shared state, latency and protecting the service itself.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Options: a central store like Redis with atomic scripts (accurate, adds a hop), local limits at limit/N per node (cheap, inaccurate), or hybrid with local token batches synced periodically. Rate limiting is per-client fairness; load shedding protects the server when overall demand exceeds capacity by dropping low-priority requests early, regardless of who sent them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Central:  node -> Redis (Lua token bucket)       exact, +0.5-1 ms, Redis is a dependency
Local:    each of N nodes allows limit/N         zero hop, wrong when traffic is skewed
Hybrid:   node leases 50 tokens, refills async   small error, low load on Redis
  • Capacity: 50k rps across the fleet with one Redis op per request needs 50k ops/s, fine for one node, but a hot key (one huge customer) is a single-shard bottleneck; fix with key splitting or lease batching.
  • Failure mode: if Redis is down, fail-open (availability) or fail-closed (safety) per route.
  • Load shedding: watch queue length, in-flight count, or latency; drop by priority (health checks and paid tier last), return 503 with Retry-After, use adaptive concurrency limits, drop before doing expensive work.
  • Pair with client-side exponential backoff and jitter to avoid retry storms.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Per-node limit of limit instead of limit/N.
  • Shedding after the work is done (wasted effort).
  • Retries without jitter turning a limit into a storm.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 429 or 503? -> 429 for client over quota; 503 when the server sheds load.
  2. Multi-region limits? -> Per-region budgets with periodic reconciliation, accept approximate global accuracy.
  3. How do you pick the shed threshold? -> Measure throughput vs latency curve; shed at the knee.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Redis". Senior: trade-offs of accuracy vs latency, hot keys, failure policy, shedding and backoff semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fail-closed limiter on a Redis blip took down the whole API for 4 minutes.

questions.contextHtml:
Login service normal: 400 logins/min, 94% success. Now:

logins/min: 38,000    success rate: 1.8%    distinct IPs: 210,000 in 1 hour (about 3 attempts each)
distinct usernames: 36,000, each tried once or twice
many usernames match a recent third-party breach list
support: 120 accounts report unauthorised gift-card purchases
per-IP limit: 20/min (never triggers); argon2 CPU: 100%

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Lowers the per-IP limit (already irrelevant: 3 attempts per IP) or blocks IPs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have MFA? Are gift cards one-click purchasable? Do we log device and ASN? Is login rate limited per account?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add friction at login (adaptive captcha or proof of work for unknown devices), per-username and global login rate limits, block risky ASNs and fingerprints, require step-up (email/OTP) for gift-card purchases and password changes on new devices, force-reset the 120 compromised accounts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) credential stuffing from a botnet with a breach list; (2) not brute force (one try per user); (3) the successful 1.8% (about 680/min) are users who reused passwords.
  4. How I'd verify: Group by device fingerprint, ASN, UA; compare usernames to known breach corpora (breached-password check); look at post-login behaviour of successes.
  5. Root cause: Password reuse plus a login that gives bots unlimited free guesses and a high-value action without step-up.
  6. Fix: Short term as above. Long term: MFA and passkeys, breached-password screening at signup/login, device binding and risk-based authentication, per-account and per-fingerprint limits, notifications on new-device logins, velocity rules on gift-card purchases, protect the hash pool with a cheap pre-check.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards of success rate by cohort and ASN, anomaly alerts, runbook, fraud-loss tracking.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Friction costs conversions; use risk-based triggers. I would not lock accounts after N failures (enables denial of service against victims); prefer progressive delays and step-up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Attacker rotates residential IPs? -> Per-IP is useless; use account, device and behaviour signals.
  • Do not reveal which usernames exist? -> Identical errors and timings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Lockout after five failures was weaponised; attackers locked thousands of real customers during a sale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Per-IP block.
  • Hire: Identifies stuffing, adds MFA and per-account limits.
  • Strong hire: Risk-based step-up, breached-password checks, lockout-DoS awareness, protects the hash pool.

questions.contextHtml:
Your Redis-backed per-API-key limiter handles 40k rps with one Redis primary (about 55% CPU). Traffic is going to 10x for a launch (400k rps). One enterprise customer sends about 25% of all traffic under one key. Gateway to Redis adds 1.2 ms p50; the product SLO budget for the limiter is 2 ms.

redis ops/s now: 40k   after launch: 400k
hot key "rl:acme": 100k ops/s on one shard
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the limiter for 400k rps and the hot key.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a bigger Redis" or "Redis cluster" (the hot key still lands on one shard).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How exact must limits be (5% overshoot acceptable)? Which limits are contractual (billing) vs protective? Is fail-open allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Prepare capacity for launch: add replicas for reads is not enough because the limiter writes; add a local pre-filter now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) the hot key saturates one shard (about 100k ops/s on one CPU thread); (2) 400k ops/s total exceeds a single primary; (3) latency budget blown by network.
  4. How I'd verify: Redis --hotkeys/INFO commandstats, load test with the real key skew.
  5. Root cause: One round trip per request to shared state scales linearly with traffic and concentrates on hot keys.
  6. Fix: Hybrid token leasing: each gateway pod asks Redis for a batch (for example 100 tokens) and serves from memory; refill when under 20%. Redis ops fall by roughly the batch size (400k rps becomes a few thousand ops/s). Split hot keys into k sub-keys (rl:acme:0..7), each with limit/k, and let pods use a rendezvous-hash assignment. Accept 2 to 5% overshoot; keep strict accounting for billing in an async pipeline. Fail open with local conservative limits if Redis is unreachable.
  7. Prevention: Per-key quota dashboards, hot-key alerts, load tests with skewed distributions, periodic reconciliation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Leasing makes limits approximate and can strand tokens on idle pods; short lease TTL. I would not run synchronous Redis calls for 400k rps, nor shard by key hash alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customer upgrades their limit? -> Config pushed via pub/sub; leases expire in seconds.
  • Multi-region? -> Per-region budgets plus rebalancing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single viral customer made one Redis shard the cap of the whole platform; leasing cut Redis load by 50x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Bigger Redis.
  • Hire: Local caching of tokens, notes hot key.
  • Strong hire: Lease math, key splitting, accuracy trade-off, fail-open and separate billing accounting.

questions.contextHtml: You receive 300 erasure requests per month, growing to 3,000. User data lives in: Postgres (3 services), Elasticsearch (search index), Redis, a Kafka topic with 30 days retention, a Snowflake warehouse, S3 log archives (400 days), nightly DB backups (35 days) and two SaaS vendors (email, support desk). Today a developer runs manual SQL for each request and misses systems. Legal says: complete within 30 days, prove it, keep invoices for 7 years (tax law).
questions.promptHtml: Design the erasure pipeline and handle the awkward stores.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete the user row." Ignores derived data, backups and legal retention.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which data must be retained by law? Do we have a central user id used everywhere? Is pseudonymisation allowed for analytics? What does legal accept for backups?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the manual process; build a data inventory first so the scope is known.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (hard parts): (1) logs and Kafka contain PII not keyed by user id; (2) backups are immutable; (3) retained invoices conflict with erasure; (4) vendors hold copies.
  4. How I'd verify: Data map per store: fields, key, retention, owner; scan logs for emails and ids.
  5. Root cause: No data catalogue and PII sprinkled across stores with no deletion contract.
  6. Fix: An erasure orchestrator: request -> a workflow that publishes user.erasure.requested to every owning service; each deletes or anonymises and acks; track state until all ack; vendor APIs called by the workflow; audit record kept without PII (hashed id and timestamps). Invoices: keep legally required fields, anonymise the rest. Logs: avoid PII in logs, short retention, or tokenise ids. Kafka: let retention expire (30 days) and document. Backups: age out in 35 days; keep an erasure ledger and re-apply deletions after any restore. Warehouse: key by pseudonymous id, delete by id.
  7. Prevention: PII tagging in schemas, CI check that new PII fields declare retention and owner, periodic reconciliation to detect leftovers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Per-user encryption keys (crypto-shredding) make deletion across backups easy but add key management; worth it for the highest-risk data. I would not rewrite backups per request.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User asks for access/export? -> Same inventory, collect and package.
  • Request volume 10x? -> The workflow is automated, so cost scales with fan-out not people.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An audit asked for proof of erasure and the only evidence was a Slack message; the ledger replaced it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Delete the row.
  • Hire: Inventory and fan-out across stores.
  • Strong hire: Orchestrated workflow with acks, legal retention handling, backup ledger, crypto-shredding option.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants a "free 30-day trial, no card needed" with 50 GB of storage and an invite-a-friend bonus. Expected 200k signups a month. Last year a similar promo lost money to fake accounts. The PM says: "Make it frictionless, but don't let it be abused."
questions.promptHtml: How do you design the abuse defences, starting from the requirement?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a captcha at signup." Ignores the economics of abuse and the referral loop.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does abuse cost per account (50 GB storage at roughly $0.02 per GB-month is about $1)? What is the acceptable abuse budget? What do abusers want (free storage, referral credit, sending spam)? Which signals do we have (email, phone, device)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable (design); plan telemetry before launch so abuse is visible on day one.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (threats): (1) mass fake signups for free storage or resale; (2) referral fraud (self-referral rings); (3) content abuse (hosting malware/piracy); (4) trial cycling with new emails.
  4. How I'd verify: Pre-launch: threat model with economics; simulate with the previous promo's data; pilot in one market.
  5. Root cause: Free value plus anonymity plus rewards means a market for fake accounts.
  6. Fix: Layered, risk-based: email verification and disposable-domain checks, device and IP reputation, phone verification only for risky sessions, rate limits per device/ASN, storage quota ramps (5 GB first, rest after verified activity), referral reward paid only when the referee becomes a paying customer (delays and caps), upload scanning, rules and ML scoring with human review queue, kill switch per cohort.
  7. Prevention: Abuse dashboard (signups per ASN, referral graph clusters), loss budget alerts, feedback loop from support.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Friction vs conversion: tune by risk score, not blanket. I would not pay referral rewards instantly nor give full quota upfront.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Abusers adapt? -> Expect an arms race; measure cost per fake account and keep it above the value.
  • Privacy of device fingerprinting? -> Needs lawful basis and minimisation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A referral bonus paid at signup funded a ring that created 80,000 accounts in a weekend; moving the payout to first payment ended it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Captcha.
  • Hire: Threat list plus layered controls.
  • Strong hire: Economics-driven, staged quotas, delayed rewards, monitoring and kill switch.

questions.promptHtml: How do you classify and handle PII in a large system: tagging, minimisation, tokenisation, logs and access?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: PII leaks mostly through logs, analytics and over-broad access, not through the main database.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Classify data into tiers (public, internal, confidential, restricted), tag fields in schemas, collect and keep the minimum, tokenise or pseudonymise high-risk values, encrypt, restrict access by purpose with audit, and keep PII out of logs, URLs and analytics by default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tier 4 restricted : government ids, card numbers, health  -> tokenise/vault, field encryption, narrow access, audited
Tier 3 confidential: email, phone, address, IP            -> encrypt, role-based access, retention limits
Tier 2 internal    : order ids, product usage              -> normal access
Tier 1 public
  • Tokenisation: replace the value with a random token; the real value lives in a hardened vault, so most services never touch PII (smaller blast radius, smaller compliance scope).
  • Logs: structured logging with a redaction layer and an allowlist of fields, never log bodies or headers wholesale; short retention.
  • Access: purpose-based, time-bound, break-glass with approval and audit; masked views for support.
  • Analytics: hash or pseudonymise ids; aggregate; strip IPs.
  • Lifecycle: collection purpose recorded, retention timer, deletion verified.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• PII in URL query strings (ends up in logs and referrers).
  • Production data copied to staging and laptops.
  • Hashing emails without a secret (a rainbow table recovers them).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Tokenisation vs encryption? -> Token has no mathematical relationship to the value; encryption is reversible with the key and keeps format flexibility with trade-offs.
  2. How do you find PII you did not know about? -> Automated scanners on stores and logs, schema review gates.
  3. How do you let support help users? -> Masked fields, just-in-time unmask with audit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "encrypt PII". Senior: classification tiers, tokenisation to shrink scope, log redaction, access governance and lifecycle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A debug log line printing the whole request body put thousands of emails and tokens into a log platform readable by 400 engineers.
